voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.

beats.vo: In caves outside Beijing, scientists once found something extraordinary: the bones of Peking Man, half a million years old — some of the most important human fossils ever discovered.
In 1941, with Japan's army closing in, American and Chinese scientists packed the bones into crates to smuggle them to safety in the United States — the last hope of saving them from the war.

The crates were handed to U.S. Marines, to be shipped out of port on December the eighth. On December the seventh, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor. The Marines guarding the fossils were taken prisoner before the ship ever sailed.
The bones never reached the ship. They were never seen again — not by the scientists who packed them, not by anyone. Decades of searching, on three continents, found nothing.
All that survives are the casts and photographs one researcher made just in time. Everything we know about Peking Man, we know from copies — because the originals are still, somewhere, missing.
